steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a computer vision paper that revisits lightweight mobile CNN design from the perspective of lightweight ViTs and introduces RepViT. Cover lightweight CNNs and ViTs, why CNNs still matter on device, the comparison that motivates our study, and our approach and headline results.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. Lightweight models and lightweight CNN design principles
2. ViTs and the push for lightweight ViTs
3. Efficient lightweight ViT designs
4. Practical problems of ViTs; case for lightweight CNNs
5. Structural similarities/differences; research question
6. Our approach: modernizing MobileNetV3-L into RepViT; results

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. Lightweight CNNs
- lightweight models: good performance, lower compute; key for resource-constrained mobile devices, edge deployment
- past decade: lightweight CNNs, big progress
- principles: separable convolutions, inverted residual bottlenecks, channel shuffling, structural re-parameterization
- models: MobileNets, ShuffleNets, RepVGG

2. ViTs
- ViTs promising alternative for visual representations
- better than CNNs: image classification, semantic segmentation, object detection
- more parameters -> large models, high latency, unsuitable for mobile
- shrinking ViTs directly -> worse than lightweight CNNs
- so: lightweight ViT design aiming to beat lightweight CNNs

3. Efficient ViT designs
- hybrid networks combining conv layers with ViTs
- self-attention with linear complexity; dimension-consistent design
- lightweight ViTs: lower latency on mobile + outperform lightweight CNNs (Figure 1)

4. Problems with ViTs
- inadequate hardware and computational library support
- high-resolution inputs -> high latency
- CNNs: highly optimized convolutions, linear complexity in input -> good for edge
- need high-performance lightweight CNNs; compare lightweight ViTs and CNNs

5. Similarities and differences
- both use conv modules for spatially local representations
- global: CNNs enlarge kernel size; ViTs use multi-head self-attention
- differences in block structure, macro/micro designs not inspected enough
- ViTs: MetaFormer block; CNNs: inverted residual bottleneck
- question: can lightweight ViT designs improve lightweight CNNs? revisit CNN design from ViT perspective
- aim: bridge gap, show promise of CNNs for mobile

6. Approach and results
- start from MobileNetV3-L (following prior work), gradually "modernize" with lightweight ViT designs
- RepViT: Re-parameterization convolutions in ViT-like MetaFormer structure, pure lightweight CNN
- beats SOTA lightweight ViTs: ImageNet classification, COCO-2017 detection + instance segmentation, ADE20k segmentation
- over 80% top-1 on ImageNet at 1.0 ms on iPhone 12, first for a lightweight model
- RepViT-M2.3: 83.7% at 2.3 ms
- RepViT-SAM: nearly 10\times faster than MobileSAM, better zero-shot transfer
- hope: strong baseline, inspire research on lightweight models for edge

This is especially important for mobile devices with limited resources, so that visual models can be deployed at the edge. Some approaches propose new architectures that combine convolutional layers with ViTs, which gives hybrid networks. Also, new self-attention operations with linear complexity and dimension-consistent design principles are introduced for efficiency. These studies show that lightweight ViTs can have lower latency on mobile devices and at the same time outperform lightweight CNNs, as shown in Figure 1.

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
In computer vision, designing lightweight models has been a major focus, so that models perform very well while costing less computation. This is especially important for mobile devices with limited resources, so that visual models can be deployed at the edge. In the past decade, researchers mostly focused on lightweight convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and made a lot of progress. Many efficient design principles were proposed, such as separable convolutions, inverted residual bottlenecks, channel shuffling, and structural re-parameterization, etc. These design principles led to representative models like MobileNets, ShuffleNets, and RepVGG.

Recently, Vision Transformers (ViTs) have appeared as a promising alternative to CNNs for learning visual representations. They performed better than CNNs on many vision tasks, like image classification, semantic segmentation and object detection. But ViTs tend to increase the number of parameters to get better performance, and this gives large model sizes and high latency, so they are not suitable for mobile devices with limited resources. One could directly reduce the size of ViT models to fit the constraints of mobile devices, but then their performance is often worse than lightweight CNNs. So researchers started to explore lightweight designs of ViTs, aiming to perform better than lightweight CNNs.

Many efficient design principles have been proposed to make ViTs more computationally efficient on mobile devices. Some approaches propose new architectures that combine convolutional layers with ViTs, which gives hybrid networks. Also, new self-attention operations with linear complexity and dimension-consistent design principles are introduced for efficiency. These studies show that lightweight ViTs can have lower latency on mobile devices and at the same time outperform lightweight CNNs, as shown in Figure 1.

Even though lightweight ViTs are successful, they still have practical problems because hardware and computational library support is not good enough. ViTs are also sensitive to high resolution inputs, which leads to high latency. CNNs, on the other hand, use highly optimized convolution operations whose complexity is linear in the input, so they are good for deployment on edge devices. So it is necessary to design high-performance lightweight CNNs, and this makes us compare existing lightweight ViTs and CNNs carefully.

Lightweight ViTs and lightweight CNNs have some structural similarities. For example, both use convolutional modules to learn spatially local representations. To learn global representations, lightweight CNNs usually make the kernel size of convolutions bigger, and lightweight ViTs usually use the multi-head self-attention module. But even with these structural connections, there are still notable differences between them in the block structure and the macro/micro designs, and these have not been inspected enough. For example, lightweight ViTs usually use the MetaFormer block structure, while lightweight CNNs prefer the inverted residual bottleneck. This leads to a question: Can architectural designs of lightweight ViTs improve the performance of lightweight CNNs? To answer it, in this study we revisit the design of lightweight CNNs from the ViT perspective. We want to bridge the gap between lightweight CNNs and lightweight ViTs and show that the former are promising for deployment on mobile devices compared to the latter.

To do this, following prior work, we start from a standard lightweight CNN, MobileNetV3-L. We "modernize" its architecture step by step by adding the efficient architectural designs of lightweight ViTs. In the end we get a new family of lightweight CNNs for resource-constrained mobile devices, called RepViT, which consists only of Re - p arameterization convolutions in a ViT -like MetaFormer structure. RepViT is a pure lightweight CNN, and it has better performance and efficiency than existing state-of-the-art lightweight ViTs on many computer vision tasks, including image classification on ImageNet, object detection and instance segmentation on COCO-2017, and semantic segmentation on ADE20k. RepViT reaches over 80% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet with 1.0 ms latency on an iPhone 12, and as far as we know this is the first time for a lightweight model. Our largest model, RepViT-M2.3, gets 83.7% accuracy with only 2.3 ms latency. When we combine RepViT with SAM, our RepViT-SAM gets nearly 10\times faster inference than the state-of-the-art MobileSAM and has much better zero-shot transfer capability. We hope that RepViT can be a strong baseline and inspire more research on lightweight models for edge deployments.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
In the field of computer vision, designing lightweight models has been a major focus for achieving superior performance with reduced computational costs. This is particularly important for resource-constrained mobile devices, to enable the deployment of visual models at the edge. Over the past decade, researchers have primarily focused on lightweight convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and made significant progress. Many efficient design principles have been proposed, including separable convolutions [1], inverted residual bottlenecks [2], channel shuffling [3,4], and structural re-parameterization [5,6], etc., leading to representative models like MobileNets [1,2,7], ShuffleNets [4,3], and RepVGG [5].

In recent years, Vision Transformers (ViTs) [8] have emerged as a promising alternative to CNNs for learning visual representations, demonstrating superior performance on a variety of vision tasks, like image classification [9,10], semantic segmentation [11,12] and object detection [13,14]. However, the trend of increasing the number of parameters in ViTs to improve performance results in large model sizes and high latency [15,16], making them unsuitable for resource-constrained mobile devices [17,18]. Although the model size of ViTs can be directly reduced to match the constraints of mobile devices, their performance then often becomes inferior to that of lightweight CNNs [19]. Researchers have therefore begun exploring the lightweight design of ViTs, aiming to surpass lightweight CNNs.

Many efficient design principles have been proposed to enhance the computational efficiency of ViTs for mobile devices [20,17,19,21]. Some approaches propose architectures that combine convolutional layers with ViTs, resulting in hybrid networks [19,17]. In addition, self-attention operations with linear complexity [22] and dimension-consistent design principles [18,20] have been introduced to improve efficiency. These studies demonstrate that lightweight ViTs [22,20,21] can achieve lower latency on mobile devices while outperforming lightweight CNNs [23,2,7], as shown in Figure 1.

Despite their success, lightweight ViTs still face practical challenges due to inadequate hardware and computational library support [23]. Moreover, ViTs are susceptible to high-resolution inputs, which results in high latency [24]. In contrast, CNNs use highly optimized convolution operations with linear complexity relative to the input, which makes them advantageous for deployment on edge devices [25,26]. Designing high-performance lightweight CNNs is therefore imperative, which compels us to carefully compare existing lightweight ViTs and CNNs.

Lightweight ViTs and lightweight CNNs exhibit certain structural similarities. For example, both employ convolutional modules to learn spatially local representations [17,22,27,21]. For learning global representations, lightweight CNNs usually enlarge the kernel size of convolutions [25], while lightweight ViTs generally employ the multi-head self-attention module [17,22]. Despite these connections, notable differences remain in the block structure and macro/micro designs, which have yet to receive sufficient inspection. For example, lightweight ViTs usually adopt the MetaFormer block structure [28], while lightweight CNNs favor the inverted residual bottleneck [2]. This leads us to a question: Can architectural designs of lightweight ViTs enhance the performance of lightweight CNNs? To answer it, we revisit the design of lightweight CNNs from the ViT perspective. Our research aims to bridge the gap between lightweight CNNs and lightweight ViTs and to highlight the promise of the former for deployment on mobile devices compared to the latter.

To this end, following [29], we begin with a standard lightweight CNN, i.e., MobileNetV3-L [7], and gradually "modernize" its architecture by incorporating the efficient architectural designs of lightweight ViTs [18,17,20,30]. This yields a new family of lightweight CNNs for resource-constrained mobile devices, namely RepViT, which is composed entirely of Re - p arameterization convolutions in a ViT -like MetaFormer structure [28,31,18]. As a pure lightweight CNN, RepViT shows superior performance and efficiency compared with existing state-of-the-art lightweight ViTs [20,21] on various computer vision tasks, including image classification on ImageNet [32], object detection and instance segmentation on COCO-2017 [33], and semantic segmentation on ADE20k [34]. Notably, RepViT reaches over 80% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet with 1.0 ms latency on an iPhone 12, which, to the best of our knowledge, is a first for a lightweight model. Our largest model, RepViT-M2.3, obtains 83.7% accuracy with only 2.3 ms latency. Combined with SAM [35], our RepViT-SAM achieves nearly 10\times faster inference than the state-of-the-art MobileSAM [36] with significantly better zero-shot transfer capability. We hope RepViT can serve as a strong baseline and inspire further research into lightweight models for edge deployments.
